revisions.body: The opening’s real test is not which slogan sounds stronger. I hear Socrates turning each thesis into a practical burden: show a condition of soul capable of making life happy for all humans. That standard makes the argument comparative and answerable; a claim about pleasure or wisdom must survive the life it proposes.

The word to listen for is “irreverence.” Socrates turns classification into a test of what deserves the highest regard, not a neutral exercise in filing concepts. One way to hear the challenge is as pressure on Philebus’s standard: if pleasure’s claim to the good depends on its unlimited intensity, can that same measure judge wisdom, knowledge, and mind? The passage leaves the question open, making the next exchange consequential.

revisions.title: Standards before ranking
revisions.body: Before pleasure can be ranked, the comparison is given a standard. Protarchus says that intellect is identical with truth—or most like and truest of all things—and that nothing is more immoderate than pleasure, while nothing is more measured than intellect and knowledge. One way to read the move is as a change in the question: not which experience is strongest, but which candidate can answer to truth and measure.
